claims.text: The application is the unit of protection.                    Veeam Kasten works at that level: it discovers applications on the cluster it runs in and protects them as whole objects                                                                                                            — stateful and stateless parts together                                                                        Application object         Veeam Kasten's application object encapsulates information about all stateful and stateless resources that make up the application       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]

The control plane is not your backup target either.                    Veeam Kasten is built to protect Kubernetes applications and cannot be used to deploy or restore a cluster's overall state, so cluster build-out stays with your infrastructure-as-code tooling       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

The word "cluster" means something different on each side of this comparison. A vSphere cluster is a grouping of hosts inside a larger inventory. A Kubernetes cluster is the entire management domain — its own API, its own accounts, its own set of nodes. Two Kubernetes clusters are two separate worlds, which is exactly why moving an application between clusters is treated as a restore operation rather than a migration wizard       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Rebuild a stateless front end from its declaration and you have lost nothing. Rebuild a database from its declaration and you have an empty database. That asymmetry is the entire reason a Kubernetes backup product exists, and it is visible in how Veeam Kasten presents a cluster: its dashboard can filter down to only the applications that have stateful services, which it defines as applications containing a persistent volume       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Veeam Kasten classifies Pods, VirtualMachines, StatefulSets, Deployments, and DeploymentConfigs as     workloads     , and treats an application as something made up of multiple Kubernetes resources and workloads together       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.303]       . So a single application card in its dashboard may account for several volumes, several network resources, several workloads, and additional configuration objects at once       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.303]       .

Do not read "StatefulSet" as "everything with data". Some modern data services are managed by their own custom controllers rather than by a StatefulSet, and Veeam Kasten added support for pre- and post-snapshot Blueprint actions for those custom-resource-managed workloads by mapping Pod and volume-claim ownership when a policy runs       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]       . The reliable signal that data is present is a persistent volume, not the controller type.

A crash-consistent volume snapshot is not always enough for a database, exactly as it is not in a virtual estate. Veeam Kasten handles that case with Kanister Blueprints, which run pre- and post-backup hooks for workloads that need application-specific work such as pausing a database before a backup or migration       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . You will meet these again when you build policies.

A         namespace          is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. (On Red Hat OpenShift, which this course also targets, the same boundary surfaces as a         Project          — Veeam Kasten's own OpenShift install instructions treat the two words as one thing, telling you to create "a project (namespace)" for the installat

That convention is load-bearing for Veeam Kasten. The platform by default equates namespaces to applications — for ease of use, for consistency with Kubernetes practice and role-based access control, and because it mirrors the most common application deployment pattern       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       . It is a default, not a cage: policies can be defined to operate on more than one namespace, or on only a subset of an application that lives inside a single namespace       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Some of the application is not in the namespace at all.                    Cluster-scoped objects such as StorageClasses and custom resource definitions live outside every namespace, and an application that depends on them needs a policy that protects both the application and its cluster-scoped resources       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.429]       .

Applications, counted for you.          Nobody registered these applications by hand. Veeam Kasten abstracts each application it has automatically discovered on the cluster it is running in       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       , then reports each one as unmanaged when no protection policy covers it, non-compliant when a policy applies but its actions are failing or have not run yet, and compliant when a policy applies and its service-level agreements (SLAs) are being respected       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       .

Discovery is the part of onboarding a new estate that costs the most in a virtual environment: finding everything, deciding what is in scope, keeping the list current as people build things. Here the inventory maintains itself, and the interesting number on that dashboard is the unmanaged count — the applications that exist and are not yet covered by any policy       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.301]       . That number is your work queue.

Stage 02 — the class.          A StorageClass is the cluster's catalogue entry: a name a claim can ask for, plus the provisioner and parameters behind it. Closest instinct: a storage policy in a virtual estate. Where it breaks: a StorageClass is cluster-scoped, so it is not inside the namespace it serves — which is why protecting an application sometimes means protecting cluster-scoped resources alongside it       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.429]       .

Stage 03 — the driver.          The provisioner named by the class does the work against the storage system. Where a platform offers both a CSI driver and an older in-tree provisioner, the CSI provisioner is the one to choose: the legacy in-tree provisioners are deprecated and will be removed in later Kubernetes versions, and claims made by them are being migrated to CSI drivers       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

In a virtual estate the storage layer is largely an implementation detail of the backup design: the hypervisor presents disks, and your backup server reads them. Here the storage layer is a first-class dependency, because the ability to take a fast, consistent point-in-time copy belongs to the driver rather than to the backup product. Veeam Kasten supports direct integration with a set of storage providers — among them Amazon Elastic Block Store, Azure Managed Disks, Google Persistent Disk, Ceph, Cinder-based providers on OpenStack, vSphere Cloud Native Storage, Portworx, and Veeam Backup — as

Two practical consequences follow. First, a storage system with no CSI driver that can snapshot pushes you onto a file-copy-based path: Veeam Kasten supports Generic Storage Backups for such systems, and the documentation states plainly that this approach is not recommended       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . Most NFS storage services on the market do not provide a CSI driver with snapshot and clone capabilities, and migrating persistent data to storage that does is the recommended course       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       . Second, snapshot limits are a design input: verify

Veeam Kasten can invoke volume snapshot operations through CSI, and three requirements have to be met for that to work: Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher, the       VolumeSnapshotDataSource        feature enabled in the cluster, and a CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Using a CSI driver with VolumeSnapshot support is described as a requirement for building a good data protection solution with Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Whether a CSI provisioner supports VolumeSnapshots may be stated in the storage vendor's documentation, and it can also be validated with Veeam Kasten's own tooling rather than taken on trust       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Run with a specified StorageClass, the primer tool — the pre-flight tool you install and run in Module 03 — runs in a Pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Module 03 covers both invocations: the basic run, and this one.

For each CSI driver, a VolumeSnapshotClass has to carry the Veeam Kasten annotation before its snapshots can be used       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . You will apply it in Module 03; recognise it here.

The annotation and class name above are quoted from the Storage Integration reference       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .       k10        appears in lowercase inside the annotation key       k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class        because that key is a verbatim technical string; the product name is Veeam Kasten.

CSI snapshots are not durable. A snapshot has a namespaced VolumeSnapshot object and a non-namespaced VolumeSnapshotContent object, and with the default and recommended deletion policy, deleting the volume or the namespace containing it cleans up the namespaced object and cascades into deleting the VolumeSnapshotContent object and therefore the underlying storage snapshot       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       . Setting       deletionPolicy        to       Delete        is not sufficient either, because some storage systems force snapshot deletion when the associated volume is deleted, and

One namespace deletion can take the snapshots with it.                    In a virtual estate, deleting a VM does not commonly reach into the array and remove its snapshots. Here the cascade is documented behaviour       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .

Veeam Kasten defends the copy it restores from.                    It creates a clone of the original VolumeSnapshotClass with the deletion policy set to       Retain       , and when restoring a CSI VolumeSnapshot it creates an independent replica using that cloned class to avoid accidental deletion of the underlying content       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]       .

Chart repository         A location Helm pulls charts from. Veeam Kasten's charts come from the Kasten Helm charts repository, which you add to Helm before installing       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Chart version and product version         The chart version selects which Veeam Kasten version you install, so pinning it is how you control what lands in the cluster       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.759]       .
Release name         The name you give the installation. Veeam Kasten's documented install names the release       k10              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .
Target namespace         Where the release's objects are created. The Veeam Kasten install default is       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

Read it as three sentences: know where the charts live, refresh that knowledge, then create a release called       k10        from the       kasten/k10        chart inside the       kasten-io        namespace. Commands quoted from the install reference       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Helm is not the only route in. On Red Hat OpenShift there are two documented methods to install Veeam Kasten — a Helm-based installation and an Operator-based installation       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.53]       . Whichever you choose, the documentation encourages automating that deployment as part of the same tooling that builds the cluster, so that after a total cluster loss you can rebuild the platform and then recover applications and data with Veeam Kasten       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .

Two version checks save time later. The Helm 3 package manager has to be in place before installing, and its version should be compatible with the version of the Kubernetes cluster you are deploying into       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       . Veeam Kasten's Helm chart can also be signature-verified with the published public key during installation       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.4]       .

Veeam Kasten does not sit beside the cluster looking in. It runs     inside      the cluster, as a set of its own services in their own namespace. The install default for that namespace is       kasten-io              [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       , and after installing, the way you confirm the platform is healthy is to watch its Pods reach a running state       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

Those services are individually named — an aggregated API service, an authentication service, a catalog service and others appear in the Pod list       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]        — and Veeam Kasten's own tooling talks about validating a cluster before installation and debugging the platform's micro services afterwards       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.866]       . Read that as a design statement: this is not one monolithic server process, it is a set of cooperating in-cluster components.

The documented validation step. All of the Pods should ultimately display a status of       Running       ; it may take a couple of minutes for them to come up       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.15]       .

It discovers instead of being told        Veeam Kasten's application object abstracts an application that has been automatically discovered on the cluster where Veeam Kasten is running, and captures its stateful and stateless resources together       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       . There is no inventory to register and no agent to push.

It speaks the cluster's own language        Policies encode business rules and translate them into the actions Veeam Kasten applies to the applications it has discovered       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.620]       . Its own objects — policies, profiles, actions, restore points — live in the cluster API like any other Kubernetes resource.

It is hardened as an in-cluster tenant        Because it runs as Pods among other Pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten Pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]       . On Red Hat OpenShift specifically, that posture has a name — Security Context Constraints: Veeam Kasten installs customized SecurityContextConstraints (SCC) to ensure that all workloads associated with it have just enough privileges to perform their respective tasks       [Src: Kast

A Veeam Backup & Replication server outlives the workloads it protects and holds its own configuration outside them. An in-cluster platform does not get that luxury: if the cluster is gone, Veeam Kasten is gone with it. That is why exported backups and a documented way to recover the platform itself matter here in a way they do not for a management server sitting on its own machine — and why the documentation is explicit that Veeam Kasten protects Kubernetes applications and cannot be used to deploy or restore the cluster's overall state       [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1090]       .
